title: States and Dirac Notation
intro: A quantum state is a unit vector, written as a ket. This page introduces Dirac notation, superposition, bases, and the difference between a global phase, which is physically meaningless, and a relative phase, which can be measured.

blocks.text: Dirac notation writes a column vector as a ket $\vert\psi\rangle$ and its adjoint, a row vector, as a bra $\langle\psi\vert = \vert\psi\rangle^\dagger$. Putting them together gives the inner product $\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle$ (a number) or the outer product $\vert\psi\rangle\langle\phi\vert$ (a matrix). The notation earns its keep because it keeps track of conjugation automatically: $\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle = \overline{\langle\psi\vert\phi\rangle}$.
For a qubit the standard (computational) basis is $\vert0\rangle = (1, 0)^\top$ and $\vert1\rangle = (0, 1)^\top$. Any qubit state is a combination

blocks.caption: A superposition. The complex numbers α and β are amplitudes.

blocks.text: It is tempting to read $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$ as 'the qubit is secretly 0 or 1 and we do not know which'. That reading is wrong, and the difference is measurable: the state $\vert+\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ gives the outcome $+$ with certainty when measured in the $X$ basis, while a coin-flip mixture of $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$ gives $+$ only half the time. Mixtures get their own description, the density matrix, on Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states).
Any orthonormal basis can describe the same state. The two used most after the computational basis are the $X$ basis and the $Y$ basis:

Changing basis means computing new amplitudes as inner products: in the basis $\{\vert e_k\rangle\}$, $\vert\psi\rangle = \sum_k \langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\,\vert e_k\rangle$. The resolution of the identity $\sum_k \vert e_k\rangle\langle e_k\vert = I$ is the same statement in operator form, and it is the most-used trick in calculations: insert it anywhere.

Multiplying the whole state by $e^{i\gamma}$ changes no probability anywhere, because every prediction involves $\vert\langle\phi\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$ and the phase cancels. So $\vert\psi\rangle$ and $e^{i\gamma}\vert\psi\rangle$ are the same physical state. A relative phase is different: $\vert0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\vert1\rangle$ changes as $\varphi$ varies, and while its $Z$ statistics stay fixed, its $X$ and $Y$ statistics move. That is how phase encoding writes an input, and why the QRC shelf's Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) finds phase-encoded inputs invisible to $Z$ readouts until they are converted into populations.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
# A qubit state as a complex 2-vector: normalise it, take inner products, and check that a
# global phase changes nothing measurable while a relative phase does.
psi = np.array([1, 1j]); psi = psi / np.linalg.norm(psi)        # (|0> + i|1>)/sqrt(2)
plus = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2)                             # |+>
print("<psi|psi> =", round(np.vdot(psi, psi).real, 12))
print("<+|psi> =", np.round(np.vdot(plus, psi), 3), " |<+|psi>|^2 =", round(abs(np.vdot(plus, psi))**2, 3))
g = np.exp(1j * 0.9) * plus                                      # |+> with a global phase
r = np.array([plus[0], -plus[1]])                                # relative phase pi: this is |->
for name, v in [("|+>", plus), ("global phase on |+>", g), ("relative phase pi on |+>", r)]:
    print(f"{name:26s} P(0) = {abs(v[0])**2:.3f}   P(+) in the X basis = {abs(np.vdot(plus, v))**2:.3f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: the normalised state has $\langle\psi\vert\psi\rangle = 1$ and overlap $0.5 + 0.5i$ with $\vert+\rangle$. A global phase on $\vert+\rangle$ leaves both $P(0) = 0.5$ and $P(+) = 1$ unchanged. A relative phase of $\pi$ (which turns $\vert+\rangle$ into $\vert-\rangle$) keeps $P(0) = 0.5$ but drops $P(+)$ to 0.

items: The input of the Fujii–Nakajima reservoir is the state $\sqrt{1-s}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt s\,\vert1\rangle$: real, non-negative amplitudes chosen so that $P(1) = s$ (The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir)).
Amplitude, angle and phase encodings on Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding) differ only in which amplitudes and phases carry $s$.

blocks.title: Same state or not
blocks.text: Are $\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle - \vert0\rangle$ (both divided by $\sqrt2$) the same physical state? What about $\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle$ and $\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle$?
solution: The first pair differ by an overall factor $-1 = e^{i\pi}$, a global phase: the same state.
The second pair differ in the relative phase of $\vert1\rangle$: they are $\vert+\rangle$ and $\vert-\rangle$, which are orthogonal and perfectly distinguishable by an $X$ measurement.
